 ## Search results
HSTU already has a strong multi-negative precedent: Meta’s released 2024 configuration uses sampled softmax with 128 uniformly sampled negatives, L2-normalized embeddings and temperature 0.05. This supports an objective-only experiment while preserving the corrected HSTU backbone; those settings are starting points, not evidence of optimality for these Amazon categories. [Official configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin). The 2024 gSASRec extended abstract offers a competing hypothesis: multiple negatives plus generalized BCE reduce sampling-induced overconfidence. Its loss can be tested within HSTU without adopting the SASRec architecture. [Paper](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf).

Sampling correction and false-negative handling address different problems. The 2025 “Correcting the LogQ Correction” paper identifies popularity bias from in-batch negatives and treats the always-present positive separately in its correction; avoid applying an assumed popularity correction to uniform sampling. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331). False-negative mitigation should first exclude the target, padding and known training-history positives, using no held-out interactions. A 2026 sequential-recommendation paper studies semantic negative filtering, but its diffusion and category/brand components exceed this objective-only experiment and the available metadata. [Paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950705126010221).

Suggested bounded comparison: existing BCE versus sampled softmax with 32/128 negatives, then multi-negative gBCE; keep one HSTU checkpoint per category. These are experimental proposals, not established improvements. A 2026 preprint cautions that more negatives can underperform larger batches under fixed memory, so measure training cost alongside pinned macro validation HR@10. Preserve seeds, routing, splits and training caps; use no test metrics. [Budget study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11061).

---

HSTU’s original paper establishes the sequential transducer backbone, but does not establish that title/description semantics learned from scratch improve sparse-item recommendation. Nearby work emphasizes aligning textual and behavioral representations: ST2SI (2025) explicitly models item transitions and addresses text–ID misalignment; LETTER (2025) combines textual and collaborative information through semantic codes and masked alignment objectives. These support interaction-grounded semantics rather than treating lexical similarity as compatibility. Neither establishes the requested from-scratch HSTU recipe. Sources: [HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152), [ST2SI](https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.171/), [LETTER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12183).

A 2026 preprint, SISA-Rec, combines gated ID/text fusion with ranking and contrastive alignment, but uses BERT text embeddings; its reported gains therefore do not validate training without pretrained weights. Transferable experimental hypothesis: retain one HSTU and represent each item as an ID embedding plus a gated lexical residual from a randomly initialized, jointly trained title/description encoder. Preserve alphanumeric model identifiers and local word order to distinguish product versions, intended uses and content experiences; supervise the shared representation through next-item prediction, optionally with a lightly weighted text–ID alignment loss. These are proposed adaptations, not demonstrated findings from the cited papers. Interactions must determine whether shared wording predicts substitutes, complements or unrelated items; titles alone cannot establish compatibility. Compare against the corrected ID-only baseline using the fixed macro validation HR@10, including sparse-item diagnostics. Source: [SISA-Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11168).

---

HSTU already incorporates learned relative-position and bucketed elapsed-time biases inside SiLU attention; temporal conditioning is native to the family ([original paper, 2024](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlresearch/v235/main/assets/zhai24a/zhai24a.pdf)). The clearest controlled evidence comes from [Scaling New Frontiers](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=e6pqwHR1Yh): on MovieLens-20M, HR@10 was 0.3376 with position+time, 0.3356 with time alone, 0.3122 with position alone, and 0.3083 without attention bias. Time supplied most of the observed benefit; position added a smaller increment. These results support testing elapsed-time conditioning, but do not establish persistent/transient interest separation or transfer to the four Amazon categories.

Adjacent evidence argues against assuming monotonically stronger recency. [Long-Term Interest Clock, WWW 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15817) retrieves older behaviors relevant to the current time and candidate, then aggregates them with time-gap-aware attention, supporting recurring temporal relevance. This is a different architecture and task, not an HSTU ablation.
